# ECOWAS targets public trust as Nigeria faces regional unity test

**By :** [Azeez Kareem](https://guardian.ng/author/itunu/)

**Date:**  13 October 2026 10:44am WAT

**Share :**

[![](https://cdn.guardian.ng/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/google-1.png)Follow Us on Google Discover](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=The%20Guardian%20Nigeria%20News)

 ![ECOWAS Parliament](https://cdn.guardian.ng/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ECOWAS-Parliament.webp) 

ECOWAS

  

ECOWAS

The [Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)](https://guardian.ng/news/ecowas-warns-west-africa-faces-growing-cross-border-security-threats/) has begun implementing a new communication framework aimed at strengthening public trust and regional cooperation, as Nigeria and other member states navigate growing challenges to West African integration.

The regional bloc launched the implementation process at a workshop in Accra, Ghana, on Monday, bringing together communication officers from its institutions and specialised agencies to coordinate public messaging under its 2026–2031 Inter-Institutional Communication Strategy and Information and Communication Policy.

The initiative, developed with support from the [German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ)](https://guardian.ng/tag/german-agency-for-international-cooperation/), seeks to improve how ECOWAS communicates its decisions, policies and achievements to citizens across the region.

The move comes as the organisation faces a significant challenge to its regional integration ambitions following the withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, which became effective on January 29, 2025.

Advertisement

The three countries, now aligned through the Alliance of Sahel States, announced their departure amid disagreements with ECOWAS over its response to military takeovers and demands for a return to constitutional rule.

Their exit has raised questions about the bloc’s ability to maintain regional cooperation, particularly on security, trade and the movement of people across West Africa.

[![EFN Non Oil Export](https://cdn.guardian.ng/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-22-at-3.28.34-PM.jpeg)](https://exportfromnigeria.info/)

Nigeria, which hosts the ECOWAS Commission’s headquarters in Abuja, has played a central role in the organisation’s diplomatic efforts to preserve regional unity. [President Bola Tinubu chaired the bloc’s 2024 summit,](https://guardian.ng/news/tinubu-presides-over-ecowas-66th-ordinary-summit/) at which regional leaders acknowledged the three countries’ withdrawal decisions while keeping the door open for dialogue.

ECOWAS subsequently announced transitional arrangements to prevent disruption to trade and travel, including continued recognition of certain national identity documents and the maintenance of visa-free movement for citizens of the departing countries pending further decisions.

Advertisement

The new communication framework could help the bloc explain such decisions more clearly to citizens and businesses whose activities depend on regional cooperation.

At the Accra workshop, Joel Ahofodji, director of communication at the ECOWAS Commission, said the priority was to move from adopting the policy and strategy to putting them into practice.

He highlighted the need to respond to changes in the digital communication environment and address emerging information challenges while supporting the objectives of ECOWAS Vision 2050.

Lilian Seffer, representing the German government through GIZ, also stressed the importance of turning the policy into practical action.

She said communication was essential to the transition from an “ECOWAS of States” to an “ECOWAS of Peoples”, in which citizens understand, trust and participate in the regional integration process.

Ambassador Mohammed Lawan Gana, the ECOWAS resident representative in Ghana, who conveyed a message from Commission President General Birame Diop, said technological advances, including artificial intelligence, were changing the information landscape and creating challenges for peace, security and regional stability.

He called for clearer responsibilities and stronger coordination among ECOWAS institutions to ensure consistent communication across the bloc.

For Nigeria, the effectiveness of the strategy will depend partly on whether regional policies are communicated in ways that citizens can understand and relate to their daily lives. Cross-border traders, transport operators, students and migrant workers are among those affected by decisions on movement, trade and regional security.

ECOWAS said participants at the workshop would review communication activities undertaken in 2026, identify lessons and align institutional priorities ahead of 2027. They would also develop ways to coordinate planned activities and address shared communication challenges.

The bloc said the process was intended to improve institutional cooperation, strengthen public engagement and make its programmes more visible.

Advertisement

However, the workshop announcement did not specify implementation budgets, measurable public-trust targets or timelines for assessing the strategy’s impact.

Those details will be important in determining whether the framework translates into sustained public engagement rather than more coordinated institutional messaging.

Established in 1975, ECOWAS has pursued regional economic integration, cooperation and free movement among West African countries. Its Vision 2050 seeks to build a more integrated and citizen-centred community.

The new framework therefore places communication at the centre of a broader challenge: ensuring that regional integration remains meaningful to citizens, even as political disagreements and security concerns test cooperation among West African governments.
